messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] Re: run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
parts:
est.map can be run using multiple processors in parallel, one for each chromosome, using the 'n.cluster' argument.

I would generally run such long-running R jobs from the command-line: put the R commands into a script file, say "myscript.R" and then type

R CMD BATCH myscript.R

You can estimate the map for a single chromosome at a time and combine them using c(). And you can use replacemap() with a map for just one or a few chromosomes.

data(hyper)
map1 <- est.map(hyper, chr=1)
map2 <- est.map(hyper, chr=2)
map1n2 <- c(map1, map2)
hyper <- replacemap(hyper, map1n2)

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
parts:
calc.genoprob doesn't have a "chr" argument but rather calculates probabilities along all chromosomes.
But you could subset the cross in advance, if you want.

You can combine scanone results for multiple chromosomes with rbind().

Here's an example

library(qtl)
data(hyper)
hyper_c1 <- calc.genoprob(hyper[1,], step=1)
hyper_c2 <- calc.genoprob(hyper[2,], step=1)
out_c1 <- scanone(hyper_c1)
out_c2 <- scanone(hyper_c2)
out <- rbind(out_c1, out_c2)

karl

I think I had suggested ordering the markers on each chromosome, one chromosome at a time.
And I would do this not by subsetting the cross, but by using the 'chr' argument in orderMarkers and est.map.

For calc.genoprob and scanone, I would work with the full set of chromosomes together.

While you can subset a cross by chromosome, I don't think there's an easy way to get them back together.
I would read in the full cross data and then re-order the markers as you'd determined them, but keep all chromosomes together.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
parts:
This doesn't really work. You want to adjust for the scan across the genome, and the procedure you describe would only control for the scan across a chromosome.

There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since

Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.

But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.

karl

On Thu, Oct 6, 2016 at 1:30 PM, Karl Broman <kbr...@gmail.com> wrote:

This doesn't really work. You want to adjust for the scan across the genome, and the procedure you describe would only control for the scan across a chromosome.

There's a way to use the chromosome-specific permutation results to get an overall threshold, but it would require more permutations since

Better would be to use set.seed() prior to running the permutations for each chromosome, to ensure that the permutations used are exactly the same for each chromosome, and then for each permutation replicate, maximize across the chromosomes.

But I think really you want to get the chromosomes together and do things in the traditional way. The results will be more easily obtained and more trustworthy.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] run est.map for different chromosomes and combine the results
parts:
What does the map look like when you read the data in?

Try summaryMap(mycross)

One possibility is that there are problems with the genotype data, with some markers having miscoded genotypes or in the wrong position, so that the inter-marker distances are greatly inflated.

But I can't tell from the information given.

est.map() is not going to return bp; it returns estimated cM positions using the available genotype data.

One other thing: you'd mentioned before that this is an F4 population. The estimated distances are then going to be inflated due to the multiple generations of recombination. But not inflated by *this* much.

karl
